title: The Development of Metacognition and Its Impact on Mathematics Academic Achievement Among Junior High School Students https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11409-026-09456-2
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), April 23, 2026 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers a 2.5-year longitudinal study by Xie, Liu, and Lei tracking 334 Chinese junior high school students to map how metacognitive ability — awareness and regulation of one's own thinking — develops and relates to mathematics achievement. Metacognition generally peaked in seventh grade before declining, and latent class analysis split students into three trajectories: a high-slow-rising group, a middle-slow-declining group, and a low-significant-declining group. While a student's initial metacognitive level strongly predicted their starting point in maths, it didn't dictate how fast they improved from there. Barton highlights the study's counterintuitive warning that high-stakes testing environments and heavy teacher scaffolding may actually suppress the growth of independent self-regulation, and draws out differentiated responses for each of the three student profiles — from assigning open-ended peer-tutoring tasks to the highest group, to rebuilding confidence through small steps and think-aloud protocols for the lowest.
points: Metacognitive ability generally peaks in seventh grade and then noticeably declines through the rest of junior high, contradicting any assumption that it develops steadily with age.
A student's starting metacognitive level predicts their starting point in maths achievement but does not dictate their rate of improvement — low starters can still improve quickly.

Highly structured, test-driven environments and heavy external scaffolding can create “cognitive dependency,” inadvertently suppressing the growth of independent self-regulation the scaffolding was meant to build.

The three identified student profiles call for different responses: open-ended peer-tutoring tasks for high performers, structured reflective tools like self-questioning checklists for the middle group, and small-step think-aloud rebuilding of confidence for the declining group.
quotes: These findings highlight the heterogeneous developmental patterns of metacognition among junior high school stu-dents and reveal a complex dynamic relationship between metacognition and mathematics achievement.
The research finds that metacognitive abilities—defined as the awareness and regulation of one's own thought processes—generally peak in seventh grade before declining noticeably in later years.
The findings reveal that while initial metacognitive levels strongly predict starting points for math performance, they do not necessarily dictate the rate of academic improvement.
The study suggests that high-stakes testing environments and external scaffolding from teachers may inadvertently hinder the growth of autonomous self-regulation.
Highly structured, test-driven environments can create "cognitive dependency" and hinder internal metacognitive development.
